articles.title: Four arrested after police officer injured in Nottingham shooting
articles.summary: The officer was shot in the foot and remains in hospital in a stable condition, police say.
articles.body:
Four people have been arrested - including a woman on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm and possessing a firearm - after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The male officer remains in hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added.

Two women, 27 and 25, and a 24-year-old man were arrested after police stopped a vehicle in the Radford area of Nottingham on Sunday evening, while a 30-year-old man was arrested in Bedfordshire in the early hours of Monday.

The 27-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

The 24-year-old man and 25-year-old woman were also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Separately, after stopping a vehicle in Bedfordshire, the 30-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Assistant Chief Constable Claire Rukas said: "A team of experienced detectives continues to work tirelessly to establish exactly what happened before, during and after this appalling incident.

"I am pleased that four arrests have now been made and hope this provides some reassurance to the public as those detained are questioned in connection with the discharge of the firearm."

A large police cordon - which was put in place in Angel Row following the shooting - has now been lifted.

ACC Rukas thanked local businesses, residents and members of the public for their patience, support and understanding while the force carried out its investigation.

"The injured officer continues to recover in hospital and is receiving support from colleagues and loved ones," she said.

"We ask that his privacy is respected at this time.

"Our thoughts remain with him, and with his family, friends and colleagues, who have all been affected by this deeply shocking incident."

On Monday, Nottinghamshire Police and Crime Commissioner Gary Godden said the officer's injuries were "not life-threatening - it's most likely to be life-altering" .

The PCC added the incident highlighted the dangers of being a police officer.

"This officer was going to speak to two individuals who were acting suspiciously, and this happened," he said.

Labour MP for Nottingham East Nadia Whittome has told the BBC she understood the officer was "now out of surgery".

She added: "This incident will no doubt will be damaging to the reputation of the city, especially because of our past, but I think that we also saw was an extremely rare incident that was the worst of our city.

"But we also saw the best of our city. At quarter to five on Sunday morning, people coming together doing everything that they could to assist and I think that we have to take comfort in that as well."

articles.title: In 2022, a Russian Orthodox priest bought a £470,000 home beside a woman who paid £260,000 for hers; their fight over a one-metre strip of land has led to CCTV, criminal charges and a holy-water blessing at the fence
articles.summary: A Russian Orthodox priest and his neighbour in West Yorkshire, England, are caught in a dispute over a strip of land barely a metre wide.
articles.body: A Russian Orthodox priest and his neighbour in West Yorkshire, England, are caught in a dispute over a strip of land barely a metre wide. The disagreement has resulted in police complaints, CCTV surveillance and criminal proceedings against the neighbour, although the case was later dropped. In an unusual development, the priest was also filmed sprinkling holy water along the fence separating their homes, an act his family says was intended to restore peace.The dispute involves Father Anatoli Vihrov and his neighbour, 45-year-old tax accountant Shamaem Burrows, who live in Guiseley, near Leeds. Their disagreement concerns a narrow section of land beside Burrows' driveway and garage, with both households maintaining that it forms part of their respective properties.According to the Daily Mail, Vihrov and his wife Elena, an NHS dentist, moved into their detached house in 2022 after purchasing it for £470,000. Burrows had bought her neighbouring three-bedroom semi-detached home in 2020 for £260,000. The disagreement arose after the couple carried out work on their garden.Four years after the priest purchased the property, the neighbours are still disputing the boundary. Solicitors have become involved, both sides have contacted West Yorkshire Police, and cameras have been installed around the properties. Burrows now wants a civil court to establish who legally owns the contested land.Two different versions of the boundaryThe disagreement centres on whether the Vihrovs extended their garden into an area belonging to Burrows. She alleges that work carried out by the couple involved digging beside her garage and driveway, affecting the supporting foundations before a patio was constructed over the disputed ground.Burrows says she has property documents from 1974 that establish the boundary in her favour. She has also placed a yellow wire between the houses to indicate where she believes the dividing line should be.But the Vihrovs say her understanding of the property boundary is incorrect. They commissioned a professional survey, reportedly spending thousands of pounds, and maintain that its findings support their ownership of most of the contested strip.They also argue that the Land Registry documents cited by Burrows do not establish the precise boundary because the plans are illustrative.How holy water became part of the disagreementAs relations between the households deteriorated, their CCTV cameras began recording incidents around the disputed area.One recording showed Father Vihrov in his religious clothing sprinkling holy water near the fence. Other footage appeared to show him moving the wooden fence and holding a saw towards a camera.For Burrows, these incidents have contributed to her concerns about the behaviour of the people living next door. “He’s been shaking the fence. He’s coming around here in full robes throwing holy water on my driveway,” she told The Sun. She also claimed that the priest's religious position influenced how he behaved towards her.His wife, however, rejected the suggestion that the blessing was intended to frighten or upset their neighbour. “My husband was blessing that area for peace, to calm everything down and to leave everything in peace,” Elena said.She explained that religious practices are important to the family and that her husband had hoped the blessing would help bring an end to the hostility.The two households have also accused each other of using CCTV in ways that interfere with their privacy. Burrows says the cameras leave her feeling watched, while Elena alleges that cameras installed by her neighbour overlook the Vihrovs' garden and have affected their children.A dispute over a bush reaches the magistrates' courtThe disagreement took a more serious turn in March 2026 when Burrows was charged with criminal damage following an allegation involving a bush belonging to the Vihrovs.The case was due to be heard at Leeds magistrates' court on September 30. However, prosecutors discontinued the proceedings because there was insufficient evidence.Burrows, who also reported being arrested on suspicion of assault and harassment, has complained to the police about her treatment.She maintains that the wider disagreement concerns her property rights and her ability to live peacefully in her home.The accountant has described the personal impact of the dispute, saying she has struggled with sleep, anxiety and emotional distress. She also reported being signed off work by her GP because of stress associated with the situation.Meanwhile, Elena says the family has tried to resolve the matter through legal channels and intends to continue following that approach. “We have tried to follow the law, and we will continue to be patient, peaceful and lawful until the end,” she said.You use AI every day. articles.title: WFP cuts aid to ‌500,000 Palestinians in Gaza amid funding shortages
articles.summary: The UN agency says funding shortages threaten to reverse ‘modest and fragile’ progress on food security.
articles.body:
The ⁠World Food Programme (WFP) has announced ⁠major cuts to its Gaza response due to a funding shortage, leaving about ‌500,000 people without critical support as much of the ⁠population of the war-ravaged Palestinian territory struggles to get enough to eat.

In a statement on Monday, the United Nations agency said it received less than half as much funding for its Palestine operation in 2026 as in previous years. It said it urgently needs a further $450 million to maintain critical operations in the occupied Palestinian territory over the next six months.

As a result, the WFP said it would reduce ⁠the number of people receiving monthly assistance in Gaza from 1.6 ‌million to 1.1 million. Rations will be cut from two food parcels per family to one, and bags of flour will be smaller.

The UN agency said it would also reduce the number of hot meals provided, from 250,000 to 150,000 a day. Families living in hard-to-reach areas, including near the so-called “yellow line” demarcating Israeli military control, will receive a hot meal every other day instead of daily.

More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, have brought the collapse of education, healthcare and the economy, while access to food, water, shelter and other basic necessities has become a daily struggle.

More than 74,245 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s health ministry.

UN estimates show more than 80 percent of people are unemployed and unable to afford fresh or protein-rich foods when they are available. Only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet while access to health services remains limited.

An estimated 1.4 million people, or 67 percent of Gaza’s population, are experiencing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. This figure is down from 1.6 million people, or 77 percent of the population, at the end of 2025, however the WFP said the improvement “remains modest and fragile.”

Funding shortfalls had already affected operations in the occupied West Bank, where the number of people receiving assistance was halved in September, from 400,000 to 200,000.

articles.title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
articles.summary: From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout — millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life.
articles.body: From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout — millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life. “I ended up in a situation where I had absolutely no money. Well, I had the money, but it was inaccessible,” said Irina, a blogger from St. Petersburg, who had not been able to access her money for four days when she spoke with NBC News last week. Irina, who like several other interviewees did not want her last name shared while speaking with a foreign news organization on a sensitive matter, said her rent was due the day the first outages happened, when she hoped “that it would be fixed in a few hours.” Days later, she still had no access to money to pay for utilities or even food for her small child. The strikes that took place over several days earlier this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers as Ukraine seeks to bring the war home for Russians. The disruption hit a myriad of services provided by Yandex, a tech giant akin to Google whose services are deeply integrated into daily life in Russia, and whose digital infrastructure is relied on by other third-party platforms. Many people took to social media to complain about not being able to order a taxi or food delivery. Others reported not being able to access their files on the company’s storage service, while some even struggled to get into their homes after their digital keys went offline. While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use. Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case. Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that the company is working to restore service. “Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.” Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between the southern city of Krasnodar and Moscow, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible. “The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has two million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before,” she added. Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages, and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights. She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them, this came from the outside.” Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, a 30-year-old barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after being unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues. She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay, but said the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account. Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they couldn’t see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He was originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening. Another driver, Valery from Krasnodar, had only been on the job for a few months, having previously worked at a packing center for Wildberries, Russia’s retail giant, whose warehouse was attacked by Ukrainian drones in July. When the Yandex outages started, he said the taxi app would show error messages or even send several cars for the same customer. While that has been largely resolved, Valery said the biggest issue for him was that he couldn’t withdraw the money that he had already earned with Yandex. “If I can’t access my pay in another week or two, I will start looking for another job,” Valery, 24, said. In addition to Yandex, the data centers of Russia’s biggest bank Sberbank and tech giant VK have also been targeted in recent days. That chaos is no accident, analysts say. “Ukraine’s campaign from the start has had as one of its objectives bringing home to ordinary Russians the fact that they are at war, and this involves consequences,” Keir Giles, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told NBC News. The aim, Giles said, is for everyday Russians to conclude that their lives are being disrupted because of their leaders’ actions in waging war. Yandex may also be a target because of its role in shaping what Russians see online, said Robert Tollast, a drone expert and researcher at the Royal United Services Institute in London. Data centers also have growing military value, Tollast added, as both sides use battlefield data to improve operations and commanders’ situational awareness, potentially with AI-assisted planning. Asked about the outages and whether the government was looking into financially assisting those affected, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was premature to talk about government support because Yandex is “facing difficulties,” but is “strong and powerful.” Meanwhile, Russian authorities were looking at protecting data centers after the “unprecedented attack,” said Minister of Digital Development Maksut Shadayev. On Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin held a meeting on enhancing the level of digital security in Russia, but Peskov said it was not linked to the attacks on data centers. Russia has increasingly ramped up its own attacks on Ukrainian data centers, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet.” Ukraine was reciprocating those strikes by hitting Yandex, he said in a speech last week, adding without providing evidence that “it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms” because there were fewer Russian bots around. NBC News could not verify if Yandex services going down had that effect. While both sides have hit data centers, Russia’s were an easier target, said Mykhailo Samus, a Ukrainian military analyst and director of the New Geopolitics Research Network. While Ukraine’s data centers are widely dispersed, many of Russia’s are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, he said, meaning a strike on a single site can disrupt services spanning transport, internet access and payments. “Very easy and very important,” he said.

Following the attacks, Yandex said its “data centers are the iron heart" of the tech giant. Sefa Karacan / Anadolu via Getty

articles.body: LUDHIANA: Khanna Police has registered a case against unidentified persons after a stone was thrown at a Kashmir-bound bus near Doraha in Ludhiana on Sunday night.No one was injured in the incident, although a window of the bus was damaged.The bus belongs to the same operator whose vehicle was attacked with bricks following a parking dispute near Karnal.The latest incident took place around 11.15 pm when unidentified person(s) allegedly threw stones at the bus in front of a private hospital in the Doraha area.Sources said one stone allegedly hit the front windshield, while another struck an emergency window, triggering panic among passengers.SP (Investigations), Khanna, Rakesh Yadav said police received information through the 112 helpline around 11.15 pm and “immediately” rushed to the spot. He said the bus, which had left Delhi around 4 pm and was headed to Srinagar, was escorted by police through the Khanna police jurisdiction as a precautionary measure.A police official said a stone was thrown at the left side of the bus, where passengers were seated, causing a crack in the window. He added that police had recorded the bus driver's statement and registered an FIR.The SP said police were probing whether the two incidents, including the one in Haryana, were connected.Police sources said investigators suspected the latest attack could be linked to the earlier dispute, rivalry among private transporters or the involvement of the same miscreants.The SP said Khanna Police were coordinating with their Haryana counterparts as part of the investigation. He added that the SSP had constituted a digital and technical team to identify those involved, while the DSP was personally monitoring the probe.The officer said police had also alerted stations along the route and ensured that the bus proceeded safely towards Srinagar. articles.title: Australian MP Helen Haines critically injured in ‘deliberate’ car ramming
articles.summary: Lawmaker was struck by a car outside her office in what Prime Minister ⁠Anthony Albanese called a ‘deliberate act’.
articles.body:
An Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines is in critical condition after ⁠being struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, in what Prime Minister ⁠Anthony Albanese called an attack.

“This wasn’t an accident. There was a deliberate act,” Albanese told national broadcaster ABC on Monday. “All of our thoughts are with Helen, her family, her friends, her team and her community at this extremely difficult time. We are praying for her full recovery.”

Police said a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV struck Haines outside her office in Wangaratta, some 200km (124 miles) northwest of Melbourne.

The 65-year-old “suffered what has been described as critical injuries”, Ashley Mason, Victoria police’s acting superintendent, said, without identifying the victim in line with police custom in Australia.

Mason added that civilians apprehended a 43-year-old male driver and handed him over to police, who found a knife in his car.

The attack comes after the federal police documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation’s politicians in recent years. Politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security.

Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”.

“I’ve expressed that concern to people in the media,” he said. “If you look at anyone’s social media feeds and look at the comments, people will say things that they would never say face to face.”

The prime minister said the alleged attacker’s motive remained unknown, with Australia’s counterterrorism squad activated.

Albanese praised Haines, whom he described as “incredibly hardworking”.

“She is fiercely intelligent but, most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being,” he said.

Her family issued a statement but said it would offer no further comment, asking that their privacy be respected by the public and the media.

“This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” it said.

“We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.”

Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.

She was widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

articles.title: US lawmakers sound alarm as violence grips NATO ally Albania amid anti-government protests
articles.summary: Student-led protests in Tirana have turned violent as thousands demand Prime Minister's Edi Rama's resignation amid allegations of corruption. Rama has blamed outside agitators for the violence.
articles.body: U.S. lawmakers are growing concerned with ongoing violence gripping the small NATO nation of Albania as police clashed with protesters in the capital Tirana. The violence continued for a sixth straight day on Sunday as the lawmakers issued warnings on social media to Albanian authorities. "The Albanian people deserve freedom, rule of law, and institutional accountability. The government must refrain from all violence against protestors. Young people deserve a voice in the future of their country," Republican South Carolina Representative Joe Wilson posted on X. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Ala., posted on X that: "All parties must reject violence, and the government must respect the rights of peaceful protesters. Albania’s young people deserve a voice in shaping their nation’s future." Aderholt and Wilson were joined by Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, who stated on X: "The protests in Albania are a culmination of the people’s distrust of corrupt politicians and fatigue over the total disregard for the rule of law." Police said 388 people had been charged with criminal offenses during the demonstrations, and an unspecified number of protesters and police have been injured, according to Reuters. The U.S. Embassy in Albania called on all demonstrators to exercise their right to protest peacefully with no violent rioting, urging restraint and calm on all sides. EUROPEAN CAPITAL ROCKED BY VIOLENT PROTESTS AS GOVERNMENT CORRUPTION PROBE FUELS UNREST Tens of thousands have protested amid allegations of government corruption, inadequate education, unemployment and a lack of opportunity. The growing nationwide protest movement is driven by students and citizens also demanding accountability, an end to corruption and what they say is the restoration of democratic institutions and the rule of law. The student-led demonstrations in Tirana, which have turned violent, have quickly spread to other parts of the country. Protesters have hurled rocks at police, burned government buildings, smashed shop windows and destroyed private property. They are demanding the resignation of Rama and have been met with a heavy-handed police presence, including rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas. Prime Minister Edi Rama is portraying the demonstrations as a threat to Albania's European future, with the country on the unsteady path to European Union membership. On Monday, Rama blamed outside forces for the violence, according to Reuters. "They are young men and women who have been ideologized and radicalized under the pressure or inspiration of that dark and new force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, which the President of the United States has designated a terrorist organization: ANTIFA." In a post on Facebook translated by Reuters on Friday, Rama said, "These are also foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace; they do not want Albania to see clearly, to move forward, or to focus daily on addressing its own challenges for the sake of improvement. They do not want Albania to be part of the united European family — a place where it could finally, once and for all, escape these hands and the yoke of a forced choice." FORMER ALBANIAN PRESIDENT ARRESTED ON CORRUPTION CHARGES, OPPOSITION CLAIMS CHARGES ARE POLITICALLY MOTIVATED "Rama's attempt to equate the unrest in Albania with the protests taking place in France, Italy and elsewhere in Europe overlooks the specific political grievances driving Albania's demonstrations," Agim Nesho, former Albanian ambassador to the U.S. and the United Nations, told Fox News Digital. Nesho said Albania's European future must not be confused with the political survival of Edi Rama or any government. "European integration is supposed to reinforce democracy, judicial independence, transparent governance, and fundamental freedoms — not provide political protection from public accountability. Brussels has a responsibility to examine allegations of police abuses independently, uphold the rights of peaceful demonstrators, and take seriously the grievances behind this national movement," Nesho added. The European Commission Directorate-General for Enlargement and Eastern Neighborhood condemned the violence gripping Albania. "We condemn the use of violence in Tirana and other cities in Albania, including arson, attacks on State institutions and the destruction of public and private property. Violence has no place in a democratic society, and the response to it must remain within the law and proportionate," the Commission said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Commission noted the important gains Albania has made toward EU membership, reminded Albanians that grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner. The turmoil in Albania comes as the country has long sought European Union membership, which began in 2014 when it became an official candidate for accession. While the 2025 annual European Commission report stated that Albania made significant strides in judicial reforms and combating organized crime, the continued allegations of corruption in the Rama government and the current violence taking place will complicate its path to EU membership. Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit
articles.summary: There have been new reports of Iranian support for the Houthis in Yemen amid a wave of attacks on Saudi cities.
articles.body:
New allegations about Iranian support for Yemen’s Houthis have emerged in media reports and official comments, highlighting the opaque nature of the alliance.

Media outlets have reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) aided the Houthis as they seized swaths of western Yemen and launched their most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia, which supports the internationally recognised Yemeni government fighting the Houthis.

Iranian support for the Houthis reported by the media includes training, intelligence, tactical guidance and help in targeting for drone and missile attacks.

If true, this will undoubtedly escalate tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia, given that the kingdom has been targeted by dozens of Houthi drones and missiles in recent weeks, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people. Saudi energy facilities and oil tankers have also been targeted by the group.

Iranian backing, according to the reports, contributed to a September offensive by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God). Those battles saw the Houthis win control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Iranian Mahan Air flights ferried IRGC paramilitary officers, drone parts, missile guidance systems and impact detonators to the Houthis in Yemen. IRGC officers were also reportedly on the front lines directing Houthi attacks.

The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, confirmed the presence of an external state actor behind the Houthis’ evolving arsenal but did not mention the state in question.

Al-Maliki noted that the Houthis, who have been at war with the government since 2014, have acquired advanced technologies with regional assistance.

This support has made the Houthis the first nonstate armed group to deploy ballistic missiles, offensive and suicide drones, and explosive-laden, high-speed boats, he said, although other Iranian allies, such as Hezbollah and Iranian militias, also possess such weaponry.

While the Houthis have stressed their independence from Iran, the two groups are ideologically aligned. They have also been accused of collaborating closely on military matters, evident in the Houthis’ missile arsenal.

Analysts who spoke to Al Jazeera all agreed that the “regional assistance” the Houthis are receiving points towards the IRGC although Iran and the Houthis denied this.

One indication of this is the bombing of Sanaa International Airport in July before an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation travelling from Tehran was due to land. The Yemeni government, which said its forces carried out the attack, accused “the Iranian aircraft” of violating Yemeni airspace.

“[Recent reports] confirm what is known to experts for years as the Revolutionary Guard and Hezbollah experts engaged in managing the operational planning of battles against the Yemeni government and neighbouring countries, including the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“For example, the killing of Hassan Irloo, the Revolutionary Guard envoy to the Houthis, in Yemen after the military campaign on Marib in 2021 is one of the important indicators, in addition to Mahan aviation flights that transported more experts ahead of the Houthis’ internal and external escalation during July of this year.”

Ali al-Dahab, a military and strategic security affairs expert, agreed that the advanced weaponry used by the Houthis indicates an Iranian role in recent operations.

“What was leaked about Iranian support for the Houthis through this report did not add anything new except that it confirmed the confirmed, and what it added perhaps is that weapons smuggling, especially precision technologies for missiles and unmanned aircraft, takes place via small submarines,” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.

“This issue is not everything being smuggled from Iran to the Houthis because there are interceptions of smuggled shipments revealed by the joint forces that were controlling the Mocha coast to Bab al-Mandeb before the Houthis’ control and before its break in September.”

Al-Dahab pointed out that while smugglers historically have used dhows, traditional wooden sailboats, to mislead naval coalitions, employing submarines is a new method used by the Houthis, akin to the tactics used by organised criminal groups in the Americas.

“It indicates that Iran focuses on the Houthis as the centre of military and security gravity south of the Red Sea and, therefore, provides them with these weapons, ammunition, expertise and information in anticipation of a battle that may break out in the Strait of Hormuz,” al-Dahab said. “Therefore, the Houthis play a supporting role for them in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.”

He warned of broader implications for international shipping with the Houthis now in control of Bab al-Mandeb, a narrow waterway linking the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea.

“The greatest danger now is that substate entities in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region unite under Iran’s leadership to confront the United States, Britain and Europe in general if a battle breaks out in the Gulf of Aden and the strait,” al-Dahab said.

Saudi Arabia and Iran had appeared to have patched up years of hostilities, including the suspension of diplomatic relations, with a China-brokered reconciliation agreement signed in Beijing in 2023.

Hesham Alghannam, a Riyadh-based fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said he doubts whether Saudi Arabia ever read the Beijing agreement as reconciliation but as a way of lowering tensions. Differences on geopolitical issues have continued between the two countries since the agreement was signed, including on Yemen, which lies on Saudi Arabia’s southern border.

“That isn’t a breach you can take to a lawyer. It’s keeping two files apart, and it works until someone says it out loud. That’s what’s changed,” Alghannam told Al Jazeera.

“Honestly, the deeper question was never whether Tehran signs [the agreement with Saudi Arabia]. It’s whether anything Tehran signs reaches the people holding the launchers,” he added, referring to Iran-aligned armed groups, such as the Houthis.

“We know how the other sequence ends. In 2014, the [Houthis] were offered seats, special status for Saada [the northern Yemeni stronghold of the Houthis] and a share of the executive authority in Yemen in return for handing the heavy weapons to the state,” he added.

What followed was the Houthis seizure of the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south, and the later killing of former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.

“What followed was the seizure of the institutions, the president detained, parliament dissolved. The gains were banked, and the guns were kept,” Alghannam added.

“Saleh partnered with them, and he was killed in the street in 2017. Even after taking Sanaa, they didn’t become the state. They built a network of supervisors sitting over every official post. So the Saudi red line is one thing, no armed group or second army inside one state.”

The Saudi-led intervention in Yemen began in March 2015 and led to another direct conflict between Riyadh and the Houthis. Despite the massive support Saudi Arabia provided the internationally recognised government, it failed to retake Sanaa. This highlighted weaknesses within the anti-Houthi coalition, including divisions between the internationally recognised government and southern separatists.

“The lesson of 2015 wasn’t that acting firmly leads to a long war. It was that announcing a goal earlier than you should [do] does because once it’s said out loud, you’re bound to it long before you can deliver it,” he said.

“What Riyadh is trying to do now is easy to say and hard to do, but it’s crucial: tie the money and the weapons to real integration under one command, not to declared loyalty.”

Hassan Ahmadian, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that Iran seeks technological independence for partners rather than perpetual reliance.

“This pattern is not like the United States pattern, which keeps whoever follows and allies with it in need of it, meaning [they have] to buy from the United States the weapons he needs, and the main weapon is basically not given to him if it is an Arab or Islamic country specifically,” he said.

“As for Iran, the ally is provided with the technology to create and produce the weapon, and this is not only in Yemen but in other regions and even in Gaza as much as possible where the technology was transferred because the view is different.”

Ahmadian said enabling Iran’s allies to produce their own weapons is a strategic move by Tehran and the Houthis are also motivated by breaking the Saudi siege on territories it controls in Yemen.

“The view is that this technology helps in confronting a common enemy, and therefore, strengthening this capability independently of Iran is in itself a strategic interest for Iran,” Ahmadian said.

“Notice that there is an advance for Ansar Allah [the Houthis] linked to the justice of the cause as there is a siege imposed on the Yemenis affecting 70 percent to 80 percent of the society controlled by Ansar Allah and the Sanaa government. So this cause, breaking the siege, is a just cause. … The regional circumstance gave [the Houthis] a motive that this is the time to pressure Saudi Arabia to break the siege, and this is what actually happened.”

articles.title: France moves to impose curfews as it reels from worst violence in years
articles.summary: Only shattered glass and the skeletal frame of the Haussmannian roof remain of Limoges’ 19th-century town hall.
articles.body: Only shattered glass and the skeletal frame of the Haussmannian roof remain of Limoges’ 19th-century town hall. The town was among the places hit hardest by the rioting and looting that erupted across France over the weekend, leaving the country reeling from its worst violence in years. The towering spire at the heart of Limoges ultimately collapsed in flames, drawing cheers from the crowd below that were captured on video. In Paris, the Louvre Museum said it was closed after protesters announced their blockade of the iconic tourist site. Authorities conceded they had “lost control” in major cities, and said Monday they had asked some cities to impose a partial curfew in a bid to restore order. “Despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed and that is a miracle,” Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said after an emergency meeting with top officials. About 3,000 businesses had been looted or vandalized, he added. The unrest came on the heels of an anti-government movement that had seen days of largely peaceful protests over rising living costs and poor school conditions. On the weekend, this unrest descended into violence on the streets of cities across France: Rioters, often hooded and masked, looted stores and torched cars and government buildings as they faced off with the police. More than half a million people took part in the protests across the country, according to the French Interior Ministry, and nearly 2,400 people were arrested. Almost 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured, it added. Macron blamed “troublemakers from far-left fringe groups” for the violence. “Watching these images, we all wondered how French people could do this to France,” he said in a televised address Sunday. “Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it.” Macron added that “those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.” Macron’s centrist administration, in its final months of power, has been consumed by a mounting sense of crisis that could pave the way for the far right to take power next year. Macron will leave the presidency of the Eurozone’s second-biggest nation with ballooned debt, stagnated growth and deep-seated social discontent. The president “looks like a spectator,” Sylvain Brouard, research director of Fondation Nationale des Sciences Politiques at Sciences Po in Paris, told NBC News. “It doesn’t look like he was in control of anything,” he said, and people are expecting “solutions.” Macron appeared at a Celine Dion concert Friday and embarked Monday for a Gulf tour to secure oil supplies, fueling criticism that he appeared out of touch with public concerns. “That’s probably a source of anger for many of the people that were claiming their frustrations and their deprivations and the need for more money for the higher cost of living,” Brouard said. As the damage became clearer Sunday, political leaders across the spectrum pointed fingers at each other for the violence. Macron’s centrist government blamed the far left, while the leading far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon blamed the incumbents. Leading far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen on Sunday called Macron’s administration “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness.” She leads the polls ahead of April’s vote. Macron stopped short of declaring an emergency, as some right-wing politicians demanded. But some cities, including the southern port city of Marseille, imposed a ban on public gatherings for most of Monday. Speaking after the crisis meeting Monday, Lecornu said he had asked some local authorities to introduce curfews but dismissed the idea of putting all of Paris under such a measure. Unrest had continued in Paris on Sunday as police faced off with demonstrators at Place de la République. Damage was acute all around France, though, not just in the capital. While protest movements are part of the fabric of French society, they seldom take a turn as violent as they did over the weekend. For many, watching flames engulf the town hall in Limoges, a central town known for its porcelain, was an assault on the state itself. “To attack her is to attack the republic,” Mayor Guillaume Guérin said in a post on X on Sunday. In the southeastern city of Lyon, a tourist office building was burned. Some storefronts along the shopping streets near Bordeaux’s city hall were destroyed, and the goods inside appear to have been stolen, social media videos geolocated by NBC News showed. City halls in Marseille, Lille, and Angers were broken into, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Sunday, adding the arrests made had little to do with the student protests. Authorities had “lost control” in major cities, the interior minister conceded. He offered his resignation to Macron, who rejected it. President Donald Trump blamed immigration for the violence in the country, saying Sunday on Truth Social, “France is burning!” He blamed immigrants again on Monday, saying, “They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” Vice President JD Vance said on X the protests served as a warning for Americans. “This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” Vance said. French officials have not blamed immigrants for the unrest. Macron acknowledged legitimate concerns of the protesters, while blaming the far left for the violence. High school students initially demanding better classroom conditions first took to the streets last month, highlighting crumbling infrastructure and insufficient teaching capacity. “We’re weeks into the movement, and the proposals of the government were pretty late and they were pretty deaf to the claims of the students,” Brouard said. Their protests were met with a forceful response from the police as riot officers launched tear gas. In the weeks that followed, the students were joined by several labor unions and farmers who demanded respite from a whole host of issues, including primarily the soaring cost of living and the price of gas, which has shot up in part due to the war in Iran. The demands of French students resemble those of their peers in Spain, Portugal and Albania, who in recent days have also taken to the streets over education conditions. In Italy, weekend protests over rising costs and public services resulted in hundreds of arrests after scenes of looting and vandalism, authorities said Monday.

articles.title: In 2015, Chicago-area communities needed protection from flooding and sewer overflows, so officials turned part of Thornton Quarry into a reservoir that can hold 7.9 billion gallons of water
articles.summary: Discover how the Thornton Reservoir, a key component of Chicago's flood management system, has successfully captured over 62 billion gallons of stormwater and sewage to prevent sewer overflows. Built in 2015, this vast reservoir serves numerous communities, showcasing innovative engineering solutions against flooding.
articles.body: The Thornton Reservoir in Illinois was completed in 2015 and occupies the northern section of Thornton Quarry, providing service to Chicago’s Far South Side and 13 surrounding suburbs, according to the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago (MWRD). The project was established under the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan (TARP), also known as the Deep Tunnel, to collect excess stormwater and sewage before it could spill into rivers during heavy rainfall. After heavy storms in July 2026, it reached 94% of its 7.9-billion-gallon capacity and captured more than 7.3 billion gallons of water. Its capacity was expanded from an original 14,600 acre-feet to 24,200 acre-feet, per the US Army Corps of Engineers.How a former quarry became a flood-control facilityThornton Quarry dates back to the 1860s, when excavation began to obtain aggregate for road and building construction. The site was highly suited for a reservoir because of its shallow underlying bedrock, which was very close to the surface. Consequently, the facility was developed in two stages, starting with Thornton Transitional Reservoir, a temporary flood-control facility completed in March 2003.Before it was decommissioned in 2022, the transitional reservoir provided flood relief for nine communities and captured more than 58 billion gallons of floodwater across 83 filling events. On the other hand, building the permanent reservoir involved extensive excavation, tunnel connections, and sealing the surrounding rock. The excavation was completed in 2013, and the permanent facility entered into service in 2015.The reservoir is a key component of a 36.7-mile Calumet Tunnel System and serves a 91-square-mile area of combined sewers. These tunnels collect excess water and funnel it to the reservoirs, where it remains until it is processed by the treatment system. Furthermore, the engineering includes concrete plugs in former mining tunnels and a roller-compacted concrete dam underneath the tollway. There is also a grout curtain created by drilling deep holes around the reservoir perimeter to seal the reservoir and contain the stored water. In addition, the system has gates which isolate tunnels from the reservoir when required.Stormwater storage and the protection of waterwaysThe main objective of the reservoirs is to reduce flooding and prevent combined sewer overflows. In older combined sewer systems, rainwater and sanitary sewage flow through the same pipes, and during intense rainfall the volume can exceed the network’s capacity . As a result, both the untreated sewage and stormwater would enter waterways and worsen the basement flooding.The Tunnel and Reservoir Plan (TARP) diverts these excess flows through dropshafts and underground tunnels directly into the storage facilities. In a controlled manner, the water is then sent to the Calumet Water Reclamation Plant, approximately five miles north of the reservoir, where it is treated before being released into the Little Calumet River. The whole point of why the system stores excess water until treatment capacity becomes available is to reduce the pressure on local sewers during storms.As per the MWRD’s fact sheet, the system has prevented any sewer overflow since 2020. The Corps stated that about 35,090 structures benefited from the reservoir’s flood-protection measures. The scale of the facility is better understood through MWRD’s comparisons, which stated that the reservoir could accommodate six Soldier Field stadiums or hold the equivalent of 144 million rain barrels. The July 2026 storms showed the importance of maintaining available storage because, although the system can substantially reduce flooding and sewer overflows, its storage is finite. In essence, if the reservoir reaches capacity, sewers can still overflow into rivers, as they did before TARP was built.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Meloni calls emergency meeting after violent clashes in Milan
articles.summary: More than 200 people were detained during two days of rioting in the city, Italian media reports.
articles.body:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan.

More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers.

"To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".

Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania.

Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".

Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".

Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported.

The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI.

Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured.

Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north.

Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.

The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting.

"Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".

Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.

The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

articles.title: On Iran, Israel’s opposition is even more hawkish than Netanyahu
articles.summary: In rest of the world, the Israeli PM is often blamed for the Iran war. His opponents say he hasn’t been tough enough.
articles.body:
When Israel launched a sweeping military assault on Iran with the United States in February, the Israeli government enjoyed overwhelming support from the Jewish Israeli public.

Opposition parties lent their support to the army and backed the audacious step. Enmity towards the government in Iran is an issue mainstream Zionist parties agree on.

Then in June, Israel’s role in the confrontation halted abruptly with an announcement from US President Donald Trump, who said Iran and Israel had agreed to stop attacking each other.

That announcement – and Netanyahu’s decision to abide by it at the time – were unpopular in Israel. According to the Israel Democracy Institute , 65 to 70 percent of Jewish Israelis believe that stopping the war did not serve Israel’s national security interests.

As Israelis prepare to vote in national elections on October 27, Iran remains an important election issue for many. Opposition parties present Iran as an example of what they say are Netanyahu’s many failures. They promise to reset security and foreign policy if they’re elected.

The frontrunner, Gadi Eisenkot, says the conflict is unfinished. While saying that a change in Iran’s government was an unrealistic goal, Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of doing little to dismantle Iran’s nuclear programme. In September at the inauguration of his new party, Yashar, Eisenkot told supporters: “Ultimately, it must end in the destruction or dismantling of the Iranian nuclear programme, a goal not yet achieved with 440kg [970lb] of highly enriched uranium already there, which could quickly be turned into several nuclear devices.”

Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, who is now the head of the opposition in the Knesset, accuses Netanyahu of a strategic failure. He recently told the Atlantic Council that toppling the administration in Tehran is a realistic objective that requires a military escalation: “What Israel should do or the alliance should do is bomb all the energy facilities, especially on Kharg Island, but other places as well in order to make sure that the Iranian economy is demolished. And the reason is that it’s the only thing that will overturn the regime.”

Bombing this civilian infrastructure was actually something Netanyahu had lobbied for himself. An international outcry about such bombings likely constituting war crimes and Trump’s refusal to offer backing put the brakes on the plan.

Naftali Bennett, another former prime minister, says Israel must ensure its military dominance over the entire region. For Bennett, toppling the government in Iran and crushing it is a must. But he says that is not enough. The right-wing politician calls Qatar an “enemy” and says Turkiye is “the new Iran”, going as far as saying that military confrontation with the NATO member was inevitable.

“We will build an alliance of moderate forces in the region against the Islamist forces, against Iran, against Qatar, Turkiye and all the radical forces. We will take proactive actions to shape the region,” Bennett recently told supporters.

Eisenkot and other opposition leaders do not rule out renewed confrontations. They focus on their confidence in the military and security establishment in assessing the dangers and dealing with them appropriately.

But opposition leaders have voiced concern that Netanyahu might resort to military escalation before the elections to tilt the balance in his favour or even disrupt them altogether – even though the prime minister said last week that he did not plan to attack Iran before the vote.

Those fears were elevated after Netanyahu posted a video from the Tel Nof Airbase warning that Israel’s enemies might attack before the elections. Other news reports said Netanyahu has shared intelligence on new threats from Iran with the US president.

Netanyahu was quickly rebuked by opposition leaders, who accused him of “political fearmongering”.

Lapid openly questioned Netanyahu’s motives. Lapid also accused him of using the Israeli military and bases as “backdrops” for election campaign videos.

Ultimately, most Israeli opposition parties and leaders aren’t opposed to war with Iran, and many are in fact even more hawkish in their approach towards Tehran than Netanyahu. They just don’t want a new military escalation before the elections.

articles.title: France unrest: PM orders curfews, hints at declaring emergency; over 2,400 arrested - top developments
articles.summary: France is tightening security measures after a weekend of violent protests over rising living costs and deteriorating public services escalated into
articles.body: France is tightening security measures after a weekend of violent protests over rising living costs and deteriorating public services escalated into rioting, arson and looting across several cities.French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Monday that he had asked local authorities to impose limited, localised curfews to prevent further violence, while President Emmanuel Macron ordered a review of security failures and rejected the resignation of interior minister Laurent Nuñez.Authorities reported that more than 2,400 people were arrested nationwide over the weekend, with hundreds of businesses looted or damaged and public buildings targeted.The government has acknowledged shortcomings in anticipating the unrest, while promising changes to policing and investigations to identify those responsible. European governments have also issued travel advisories urging their citizens in France to avoid demonstrations and large gatherings.French PM orders localised curfewsPrime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Monday that he had asked some municipalities to introduce partial curfews following the weekend's violent protests.According to the news agency Associated Press (AP), Lecornu instructed prefects to impose “very limited” and “localized” curfews in cities to prevent further rioting and looting.Speaking after an emergency meeting with senior government officials, Lecornu said: “On Saturday, despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle.”He defended the work of police officers who faced violent groups and said he was fully resolved to restoring public order.Lecornu also said that furlough measures would be available to businesses affected by the protests from Tuesday onwards. He added that the government had no plans to cancel the Paris Saint-Germain-Barcelona football match scheduled for Tuesday.The prime minister said a state of emergency remained an option if the situation warranted it: “If declaring a state of emergency is deemed necessary, we would do so.”Macron rejects interior minister's resignationPresident Emmanuel Macron has rejected interior minister Laurent Nuñez's resignation following the violence, saying continued leadership of law enforcement was necessary during the current situation.Nuñez offered to resign over the weekend's rioting and looting but Macron refused, according to a statement from the French presidency.The president instructed Nuñez to “take all necessary steps to ensure full transparency about the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that led to the violence”.Macron also called for “new policing tactics on the ground as quickly as possible” to prevent further violent incidents.Nuñez acknowledged shortcomings in the authorities' preparations, saying there had been a “lack of anticipation” in deploying security forces. He said the police response needed to adapt to “extremely mobile groups” of rioters.“I submitted my resignation because I am responsible for everything that is happening,” Nuñez said on France Inter radio on Monday.He added, “Now, the real issue is ensuring that this doesn’t happen again. … We obviously need to be better at anticipating the kind of mobilization that is unfolding.”Nuñez also acknowledged that police had lost control in some major cities on Saturday, telling the broadcaster: “You can’t look shopkeepers in the eye when hundreds of businesses have been looted and say we haven’t lost control in some of these major cities. Obviously.”More than 2,400 arrestedThe unrest affected Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Limoges and other French cities, with groups of people setting fires, looting shops and targeting public buildings.Authorities said demonstrators and groups of rioters attacked city halls and other public offices.People set fire to rubbish bins, bicycles and other objects in Paris on Sunday, while businesses were looted in several cities.In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building. In Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into the City Hall lobby, while a police station was damaged. A fire also broke out inside a tourist office in Lyon.More than 2,400 people were arrested nationwide, according to figures reported by AP. Justice minister Gérald Darmanin put the number taken into police custody over the weekend at more than 2,330, with around 70% of them adults.Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said around 30 shops had been targeted in the capital on Sunday, describing the scenes as “unbearable”. More than 2,000 shops were expected to have been affected across France, with damage estimated at hundreds of millions of euros, according to Alain Di Crescenzo, president of the chamber of commerce.The unrest also caused injuries. Almost 1,000 members of the security forces were injured. A 17-year-old girl lost an eye during protests in eastern France, while another young demonstrator lost a hand in Saint-Étienne.Police use of grenades and other crowd-control weapons has also come under scrutiny.Marseille bans public gatherings Authorities in Marseille imposed a ban on public gatherings and demonstrations from noon to 8 pm local time on Monday following violent protests and looting over the weekend.The measure was announced by the local administration.Olympique de Marseille said its official store on La Canebière, the city's historic main avenue, had been looted during the unrest. The Ligue 1 club condemned the incident and expressed solidarity with Puma, its partner operating the store.“These events have caused significant property damage, forcing the club to temporarily close this store to the public,” the club said in a statement, adding that supporters could continue visiting its other official stores in Marseille.The planned visit to Marseille by Nuñez on Monday was also cancelled, according to Reuters, citing his entourage.Meanwhile, Darmanin said the unrest had exposed weaknesses in how security services dealt with threats posed by far-left protesters.“The security services are very good at dealing with threats from terrorists and organised crime groups, but less so regarding such far-left protesters,” he said, according to Reuters.“Clearly, it is not tackling the far-left effectively,” Darmanin told France 2 television.Government officials have blamed much of the violence on far-left activists and groups of looters. However, the reports provided no official link between immigrants and the rioting.Paris police set up special task force to identify those involvedThe Paris Police Prefect has announced a dedicated task force to investigate violence and vandalism in the Paris metropolitan area.The task force was ordered by Paris Police Prefect Patrice Faure and became operational on Monday. It brings together investigators from four territorial police forces.The team will examine reports and available footage from surveillance cameras, shop cameras and social media to identify those involved in the violence.“Their mission: to comb through all reports and all available images, whether they come from video surveillance, shop cameras, or social media networks,” the police prefect's account said in a post on X.Faure said the response would focus on maintaining a visible police presence, arresting people caught committing offences and pursuing follow-up investigations under the authority of prosecutors.“I say it clearly to the vandals: our investigators will mobilize all the technical means at their disposal to identify and track you down,” the statement said.The prefect also urged witnesses to send police videos that could help identify those responsible.Separately, French Senate President Gérard Larcher expressed solidarity with police officers, firefighters, municipal workers and shopkeepers affected by the violence. overall travel guidance for France remained unchanged.Netherlands: Its travel advisory, last updated on October 7, warned visitors to avoid protests.Nordic countries: Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Norway issued advisories urging their citizens in France to avoid demonstrations and follow local authorities' guidance.The European Union also said the right to peaceful protest must be protected, while describing arson, looting and attacks in France as unacceptable.Macron faces criticism as political leaders trade accusationsThe violence has triggered criticism of the government's handling of public order, with political leaders trading accusations over the unrest.Macron, in a televised address on Sunday, condemned what he described as “unrestrained violence” by “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals”.“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” he said.The businesses.Far-right leader Marine Le Pen criticised Macron's government as “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness”.Far-left student organisations and activists seeking to revive the “Yellow Vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 over social injustice.Authorities estimated that around 550,000 people took part in Saturday's Monday aimed at securing oil and diesel supplies and strengthening economic and defence partnerships.Macron arrived in Kuwait, where he was welcomed by Emir Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah. He is also scheduled to visit the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar by Wednesday.Before departing, Macron said the trip was needed to “secure our supplies”, pointing to demonstrators' concerns about fuel prices.The French presidency said the aim was to secure commitments on oil and diesel volumes. articles.title: Ancient DNA challenges theories about when humans first reached North America
articles.summary: University of Kansas researchers reviewed ancient DNA and 23,000-year-old White Sands footprints to trace early human migration into North America.
articles.body: Researchers examining ancient DNA have narrowed down the timeline of early human migration into North America — shedding light on a question that's puzzled scientists for decades. The study, published online ahead of its appearance in the December 2026 issue of the journal Current Opinion in Genetics & Development, looked at previously published genetic and archaeological evidence to better understand when humans first arrived in the Americas. Genetic evidence most strongly supports humans reaching the Americas between 14,000 and 20,000 years ago, the study suggests — with an arrival before 15,000 years ago considered likely. CAVE DISCOVERY PUSHES BACK EVIDENCE OF HUMAN ANCESTORS USING FIRE TO 1.79M YEARS AGO Previously, scientists thought the first humans arrived in North America roughly 13,500 years ago, a theory known as "Clovis First." Later archaeological discoveries have challenged that timeline, suggesting humans may have reached North America thousands of years earlier. The researchers, led by Bethany Potter and Savannah Hay of the University of Kansas, reviewed existing ancient DNA and archaeological evidence, including 23,000-year-old human footprints found at White Sands National Park in New Mexico. The footprints suggest humans may have inhabited North America earlier than the timeline supported by currently available genetic evidence. DNA FROM THOMAS JEFFERSON'S HAIR DELIVERS COMPELLING NEW EVIDENCE IN CENTURIES-OLD PATERNITY MYSTERY Such early populations could have belonged to genetic lineages that have not yet been sampled or that left no surviving descendants, the researchers said. By comparing previously published genetic data from ancient human remains in Asia and the Americas, researchers examined shared ancestry to trace how early Indigenous populations split into distinct groups. Some ancestral lineages diverged roughly 21,000 years ago, according to the review. The researchers also highlighted evidence that ancestral Native American populations split into northern and southern groups roughly 15,500 years ago, likely south of the massive ice sheets that once covered much of North America. articles.title: Ex-world champion boxer Liam Smith 'punched man on floor' in alleged attack
articles.summary: Smith, from Liverpool, is alleged to have inflicted serious facial injuries on a concierge worker.
articles.body:
Former world champion boxer Liam Smith is alleged to have punched a man in the head as he lay on the floor "unable to stand", a court heard.

Smith, who held the WBO light-middleweight title from 2015 to 2016, appeared for the first time at Manchester Crown Court earlier to face a charge of causing grievous bodily harm with intent.

The 38-year-old, from Liverpool, was not asked to enter pleas to the charge which followed his arrest for the alleged attack on a concierge worker at The Blade tower block on Silvercroft Street, Deansgate, on 13 September.

Alleged victim Laurent Nke suffered facial injuries and spent time in hospital, the court heard.

During a brief hearing Judge Tom Gilbart referred to the fact the incident was captured on CCTV cameras.

He said: "Part of the footage shows the defendant deliver two strikes to the head of somebody lying on the floor who's unable to stand."

He added that the cameras also recorded Smith allegedly "pushing past people to resume the incident, punching someone on the floor".

Judge Gilbart adjourned the hearing until 28 November. Smith was told to be ready to enter his pleas on that date.

The fighter, nicknamed 'Beefy', was granted bail with conditions not to contact Nke or to enter Manchester, unless to attend court, or for appointments with his solicitor.

Judge Gilbart fixed a provisional trial date for the week commencing 15 March 2028.

Smith, now of Formby in Sefton, was due to make a comeback in a fight on 4 September in Finland, but pulled out due to a calf injury, according to reports.

Smith, one of four brothers who all boxed professionally and all won titles at British level, has fought some of the biggest names in the sport including a defeat to Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez.

More recently he fought British rival Chris Eubank Jr twice, defeating him in the first fight in January 2023, before suffering a defeat in the rematch eight months later.

articles.title: The night watch: Palestinians protecting their homes from settler pogroms
articles.summary: Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are organising to protect themselves from settler attacks.
articles.body:
The life of 32-year-old Abdul Rahman Jabr changed more than a year ago when his home in the village of al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank was targeted by Israeli settlers . After the attack, he put up barbed wire in an attempt to fend off future settler pogroms .

The house, built by Abdul Rahman in early 2023 before his marriage, is located on the outskirts of the village in an area with a long history of settler violence. He now lives there with his wife and their two-year-old daughter, but settler attacks on his home and his neighbours have intensified over the past year.

His vehicle was set on fire by settlers in April 2024, and his home’s windows were smashed with stones. He cannot count the number of times his home has been targeted. In the past week alone, settlers reached his property seven times, which forced him to miss work to stay at home to protect his wife and child.

“I thought about my wife and child. How could I protect them from the settlers when there is no protection for us? I began surrounding the house with barbed wire and an iron fence. This isn’t a sufficient measure, but it’s the only thing I can do on my own,” he told Al Jazeera.

“All the neighbouring households have had to install these fences to protect themselves. We’ve made countless appeals, but no one listens, so we had to take this step. At the very least, it has helped keep their livestock away from our yards.”

Abdul Rahman’s experiences are not unique. They are part of a rapid rise in settler activity across the West Bank since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

Settlers carried out 14,742 attacks against Palestinians, their land or properties from October 7, 2023, to October 4, 2026, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, which is part of the PLO.

In the first seven months of 2026 alone, the commission recorded 4,113 attacks, ranging from assaults on people to vandalism of orchards. This was a 63 percent increase compared with the same period in 2025, and this month saw a spate of attacks on Palestinian farmers as they harvested olives.

Palestinians are now beginning to organise to protect their families and homes from settler attacks.

In the town of Sinjil, north of Ramallah, a group of young Palestinian men have repelled several settler attacks in recent months. Basel Awad, a pseudonym used for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that the village’s guard committee, which he is a member of, is unofficial and intended to protect the homes of residents.

Each night, 20 to 30 unarmed people gather at key locations that settlers have used as staging posts for their raids into Sinjil.

They have paid a high price for their efforts. The Israeli army has arrested six members of the guard and at least 10 have been injured in an apparent bid by Israel to dismantle this neighbourhood watch.

“We had set up a tent in the Jabal al-Batin area, which is frequently targeted by attacks. Soldiers arrived last winter and fired tear gas canisters inside. We all suffered from suffocation, and then they demolished the tent and confiscated it,” Basel told Al Jazeera.

Despite the dangers, Palestinians are refusing to leave their homes and have their land seized by settlers.

Nasr Radwan, 53, is one of the landowners in the village of Beitillu, west of Ramallah, whose property is frequently raided by settlers. The land owned by Nasr, his brothers and their relatives spans 1,500 dunums (1,000sq metres or a quarter of an acre) and contains more than 100 springs.

He has been beaten by settlers on several occasions, but he and his brothers insist on being present on the land every single day.

In June, settlers established an outpost near his land, which is being used as a base to attack his crops and assault his family, he said.

“The most recent attack took place last Saturday. We were on our land harvesting olives when settlers attacked us, smashed the windows of our vehicles and beat my brother. Even so, we continue to go there every day,” he added.

For the past three years, settlers have tried to seize the family’s land, blocking an access road to prevent Nasr and his relatives from reaching it by car. Family members persist, travelling 5km (3 miles) on foot to reach their land.

“We know that being on our land means facing constant attacks. It could even cost us our lives. But we also know that if we abandon it, it will be lost forever,” he said.

“This is not just land or a source of livelihood; it is our soul, our memory and our very life.”

With the settler raids sanctioned by Israeli authorities, Palestinian residents have no real protection or recourse for legal action when they are attacked. This has left West Bank villages exposed to continual assault with no penalties for settlers who destroy, assault or sometimes kill.

Human Rights Watch in August reported that Israeli authorities have failed to prosecute settlers for acts of violence committed against Palestinians. By the end of 2025, the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din reported that out of hundreds of cases it has documented since 2005, only 3 percent have resulted in convictions. The village watch scheme is an attempt by Palestinians to mitigate these risks.

Omar Rahhal, director of the Ramallah-based SHAMS Center for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that the fact that Palestinians resort to self-protection measures against settler attacks doesn’t absolve Israel as an occupying power of its legal responsibility under the Fourth Geneva Convention to protect civilians.

He said such measures are merely a stopgap solution to the settler dilemma for Palestinians, who are faced with a profound power imbalance. An illustration of this is the presence of Israeli soldiers as settlers attack their families and raze their lands.

“Impunity, the arming of settlers, the allocation of funds to settlements and policies adopted by ministers in the Israeli government are factors that contribute to the continuation of attacks and the resulting increase in the number of victims,” he said.
